newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - S.Electric profits slip, mulls payout.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - S.Electric profits slip, mulls payout.

text.p: British regional electricity company Southern Electric Plc said on Thursday it was poised to return about 180 million pounds ($302.2 million) to shareholders as it posted an expected dip in first-half profits.
The cash-rich electricity supplier's pretax profits slid to 112.2 million pounds in the six months to September 30 from 118.7 million pounds in the year-ago period.
The results, sapped by mandatory distribution price cuts that took effect in April, fell within analysts' forecast range of 102 million to 120 million pounds.

"We are very pleased with the results. Our operating profit was up 6.5 percent, despite the impact of the price review which is cutting distribution revenue," finance director Ian Marchant told Reuters in an interview.
The company, which operates in central southern England, said it planned to return about 10 percent of the value of its share capital to shareholders by March 1997.
"We'll be getting 180 million pounds to shareholders' hands some way or another," Marchant said, noting that possible options included a share buyback or a special dividend.
"We're looking at a number of ways that we can achieve that efficiently and fairly and expect to make an announcement in the next couple of weeks," he added.
Southern boosted its half year dividend to 12.9 pence from 11.3p per share and said it planned a total dividend of 43 pence per share for the year, up 10 percent from last year.
The company predicted it would keep growing dividends by five to eight percent in real terms until the year 2000.
Southern's shares traded flat at 687.5 pence at midday as its earnings, outlook and plans to reduce its cash mountain failed to impress the market.
"The operating profits increased, but not massively. And the dividend was high, but still there's more they can do with their cash," said analyst Simon Champion at Charterhouse Tilney.
"Even after the return of value, they're still going to be sitting on a lot of cash," he added.
Southern, whose attempts to tie-up with its neighbouring water company Southern Water and generating giant National Power have been foiled, said it had no further plans for mergers or acquisitions.
"Given the (regulatory) environment and the political scene we're facing, we do not believe that a deal is currently feasible for us," Marchant said.

"But we do not need to do a deal. We've got good growth prospects in all our core businesses and we're committed to growing organically," he added, noting the company planned to invest 700 million pounds over five years in its network.

Southern Electic's expansion plans include boosting its supply business and making additional investments in two generation plants. Proposals for a further three generation sites in its region were well-advanced, Marchant said.
He added that the company expected to agree early next year to an electricity supply deal that would be similar to its recent 15-year agreement with nuclear power generator British Energy Plc.
"The principal advantage is that it gives us secure access to competitively-priced generation," he said.
The company said it planned further price reductions for domestic customers from April of next year.
Marchant declined to disclose the size of the cuts, but he noted that they would result in total savings of more than 20 percent in real terms for customers over the past six years.
